steps.title: Welcome to Rocket Lab
steps.body: Build a flight-ready rocket, check its engineering, pass preflight, and enter a safe Earth orbit. Compatible parts snap into the highlighted assembly area.

steps.title: Choose a command pod
steps.body: Command pods protect the crew and flight computer. Open the Pods cabinet.

steps.title: Fit the command pod
steps.body: Drag the command pod to the POD mount. Follow the animated marker, then perform the drag yourself.
steps.hint: Drag the highlighted pod onto its matching mount.

steps.title: Add propellant
steps.body: Fuel tanks carry propellant and add liftoff mass. Open the Fuel cabinet.

steps.title: Fit a large tank
steps.body: Drag the large tank to the TANK mount. More fuel adds delta-v, but the empty tank still has mass.
steps.hint: Drag the highlighted tank onto its matching mount.

steps.title: Choose an engine
steps.body: Engines turn propellant into thrust. Open the Engines cabinet.

steps.title: Fit the launch engine
steps.body: Drag the engine to the ENGINE mount. A launch rocket needs a thrust-to-weight ratio above 1 to overcome gravity.
steps.hint: Drag the highlighted engine onto its matching mount.

steps.title: Read the engineering panel
steps.body: Fuel is usable propellant. Mass includes the fueled vehicle. TWR compares thrust with weight; above 1 permits liftoff. Delta-v measures the ability to change velocity. Budget tracks cost.

steps.title: Prepare the rocket
steps.body: A valid build displays GO. Prepare Launch checks the rocket again before leaving the lab.

steps.title: Preflight review
steps.body: Preflight reviews the key numbers and mission rules. This is normally your last chance to edit the rocket.

steps.title: Commit the launch
steps.body: This tutorial starts in a safe circular orbit so you can focus on the simulator controls.
steps.hint: Press Launch to open the flight deck.

steps.title: Orbit is continuous free fall
steps.body: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the planet. Tangential velocity carries the craft around Earth while gravity bends its path. The map shows its trajectory.

steps.title: Apogee, perigee, AP, and PE
steps.body: Apogee is an Earth orbit's highest point; perigee is the lowest. Their general names are apoapsis (AP) and periapsis (PE). A PE above the atmosphere makes the orbit safe.

steps.title: Ignite the engine
steps.body: Ignition applies thrust where the rocket points. Burning with your motion raises orbital energy; burning against it lowers energy.

steps.title: Control thrust with throttle
steps.body: Throttle controls engine thrust. High throttle changes velocity and burns fuel quickly; low throttle allows finer corrections.

steps.title: Steering changes the burn direction
steps.body: Use A/D or the arrow keys to rotate in normal missions. Radial velocity moves toward or away from the planet; tangential velocity moves around it. Keep PE above the surface.

steps.title: Cut off the engine
steps.body: Coasting saves fuel and reveals the resulting orbit. Time warp requires the engine to be off and the trajectory to be safe.

steps.title: Advance the simulation
steps.body: Time warp speeds up orbital coasting. Return to 1× before steering or firing the engine.

steps.title: Pause when you need time
steps.body: Pause freezes the simulation but leaves instruments readable. Use it before precise burns or while studying telemetry.

steps.title: Resume flight
steps.body: Resume when your next maneuver is planned. The help button opens the field manual during normal missions.

steps.title: Parameters used by later missions
steps.body: Altitude measures height above the surface. Fuel limits delta-v, while Isp measures engine efficiency. Staging drops empty mass and needs separators. Landings track speed, tilt, and legs; flybys track closest approach and payload.

steps.title: Guided orbit complete
steps.body: You built a rocket, passed preflight, controlled its engine, read an orbit, and used time warp. Reopen Guided Tutorial anytime for a refresher.
